title: Serving runtime — architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling playbook, benchmarking suite, release notes, known issues, and runbooks
author: Ava Martinez
content:
Summary:
This document consolidates the serving runtime reference material for Redwood Inference: runtime architecture, kernel scheduling design, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite, recent release notes, known issues, and operational runbooks. It is intended for engineers on the serving-runtime team, SRE, and platform owners.

1) Introduction
The serving runtime provides the high-throughput, low-latency execution environment used by Redwood Hosted API, Dedicated, and Private deployments. Key goals: predictable latency, efficient GPU utilization, safe graceful degradation, and simple operational procedures for profiling and debugging.

2) Architecture overview
- Services and components:
  - runtime-service: core request processing, token generation loop, KV cache management.
  - request-router: policy-based routing (latency/cost/region/customer-tier).
  - kernel-selector: picks vendor-specific kernels and launch parameters (cuBLAS/cutlass custom kernels, direct-attention kernels).
  - scheduling-daemon: global scheduler that assigns requests to GPU workers and enforces batching windows.
  - batcher: per-worker batching layer with adaptive batch sizing.
  - kv-cache: per-tenant/ per-model KV cache service (in-memory with eviction policies).
  - profiler-agent: lightweight sampling profiler deployed on each host.
  - bench-runner: orchestrates benchmarking jobs (latency, throughput, memory).

- Data flow (high level):
  1. request-router receives API call -> routes to appropriate runtime cluster.
  2. runtime-service performs model lookup, loads kernel profile from kernel-selector.
  3. scheduling-daemon places request in a worker queue; batcher groups compatible requests.
  4. worker executes kernels on GPU, updating KV cache and streaming results back.

- Deployment topology notes:
  - Hosted: multi-tenant pools with strict resource isolation at request-router and per-tenant KV namespaces.
  - Dedicated/Private: single-tenant pools with optional on-host HSM and KMS integrations.
  - Autoscaling: controller monitors p99 latency, queue depth, and GPU utilization.

3) Kernel scheduling design
Objectives: maximize throughput while meeting per-request latency SLOs and minimizing GPU fragmentation.

- Scheduling primitives:
  - Request affinity tags: (model-version, sequence-length-class, quantization-profile).
  - Preemption policy: short preemption windows for low-latency requests; long-running batched jobs yield to latency-critical work.
  - Kernel packing: co-locate independent kernels to reduce kernel-launch overhead when memory allows.

- Scheduler algorithm (summary):
  1. Classify incoming request (latency-critical vs batchable) using heuristics and SLA metadata.
  2. If latency-critical, schedule on reserved low-latency slots (small batch sizes, high priority).
  3. Otherwise, place in adaptive batching queue; batch size grows until either max_batch or max_latency_window trigger.
  4. On batch dispatch, consult kernel-selector for best kernel variant (FP16/INT8/direct-attn) given model and sequence length.

- Tuning knobs and config examples (table):
  - max_batch_size: 64
  - max_latency_window_ms: 50
  - low_latency_slot_fraction: 0.1
  - kernel_selection_timeout_ms: 5

Example scheduler CLI snippets:
- Dump queue stats:
  $ ri-admin scheduler status --cluster serving-prod --format json
- Force re-evaluate scheduling policy for model:
  $ ri-admin scheduler policy apply --model redwood-30b --policy low-latency

4) Profiling playbook (step-by-step)
Purpose: collect targeted traces and perf counters to diagnose latency spikes, kernel regressions, and memory-pressure issues.

- Quick checklist (preparation):
  - Identify affected cluster and timeframe.
  - Reproduce (if possible) with bench-runner in staging using representative prompt sets.
  - Ensure profiler-agent is enabled on hosts (profiling-agent-config has enable=true).

- Live profiling steps:
  1. Enable sampling profiler on node(s):
     $ ri-profiler start --nodes n1,n2 --duration 300s --output /tmp/profile-$(date +%s).pb
  2. Collect GPU telemetry (NVIDIA DCGM / ROCm counters):
     $ dcgmi dmon -e 1000 -c 5 --output /tmp/gpu-dmon.csv
  3. Record kernel launch logs at DEBUG for kernel-selector:
     set LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG && ri-service logs runtime-service --since 10m --filter kernel-selector > /tmp/kernel-logs.txt
  4. Aggregate profiles and analyze with perf-viewer:
     $ perf-viewer analyze /tmp/profile-*.pb --gpu /tmp/gpu-dmon.csv --out /tmp/prof-report.html
  5. Follow actionables: adjust batcher knobs, update kernel selection table, or submit kernel regression ticket.

- When to escalate:
  - p99 latency > SLO for 3+ hours across multiple clusters.
  - New kernel variant increases average GPU SM utilization > 15% and latency regresses.
  - Memory OOMs or kernel timeouts observed in kernel logs.

5) Benchmarking suite
Goals: provide reproducible latency and throughput metrics across models, sequence lengths, batch sizes, and quantization profiles.

- Bench-runner components:
  - workload-definitions/: YAML manifests describing model, prompt set, seq-lens, batch sizes.
  - runner: coordinates jobs, collects metrics, uploads results to S3.
  - analysis: scripts that compute cost/token, tokens/sec, latency percentiles.

- Representative workloads to maintain in repo:
  - chat-standard: mixture of short prompts (avg 30 tokens) and continuations.
  - long-context: synthetic prompts for seq=4096 and 8192.
  - embeddings-bulk: concurrent embedding requests for throughput testing.

- Example workload YAML (text):
  model: redwood-7b-v2
  sequences: [32, 128, 512]
  batch_sizes: [1,8,16,32]
  quant_profiles: [fp16, int8]
  repeats: 5

- Bench procedure:
  1. Reserve a clean GPU node image with pinned CUDA and driver.
  2. Run bench-runner with workload manifest:
     $ bench-runner run --manifest workloads/chat-standard.yaml --out /tmp/bench-results.json
  3. Upload and annotate results: attach to benchmark run in the console and link to PRs.

- Expected outputs and KPIs:
  - p50/p90/p99 latency tables for each batch/seq.
  - tokens/sec and tokens-per-dollar estimates.
  - kernel-level breakdown (compute vs memory vs IO).

6) Release notes (recent changes)
- 2026-12-15: kernel-selector v2.4 released. Improved INT8 kernels for redwood-30b: 12% p99 latency improvement for seq<=512. Added kernel selection cache to reduce kernel_selection_timeout_MS.
- 2026-10-03: scheduling-daemon: adaptive batching algorithm update (merge windows reduced from 60ms -> 50ms) and low-latency slot tuning.
- 2026-08-02: profiler-agent v1.7: lower overhead sampling mode, added ROCm counters support.

7) Known issues and workarounds
- Issue: occasional p99 spikes for redwood-30b on hosts with mixed-generation GPUs.
  - Symptoms: p99 latency spikes for short prompts; GPU SM utilization low but latency high.
  - Root cause: suboptimal kernel chosen on older GPU; kernel-selector favored a kernel variant with high per-token overhead.
  - Workarounds: pin kernel-variant in model profile or route traffic to homogeneous pools. Permanent fix: kernel-selector policy update (see ticket #INF-1143).

- Issue: KV cache eviction storms during autoscaling events.
  - Symptoms: transient latency increases and cache-miss rate spikes after scale-down.
  - Workaround: increase kv-cache-retention-ms to 120000 for affected tenants and schedule scale-downs during low-traffic windows.

8) Runbooks (operational procedures)
- Runbook: p99 latency regression (owner: runtime-sre)
  1. Verify SLOs and alert details in PagerDuty.
  2. Check cluster-wide metrics: queue depth, GPU utilization, kernel error rates.
  3. Run bench-runner in staging with representative prompt set.
  4. If reproducible, run profiling playbook and open regression ticket.
  5. If not reproducible, scale up low-latency slots and monitor for 30 minutes.

- Runbook: kernel timeout / OOM (owner: serving-runtime oncall)
  1. Identify failing host and isolate from load via request-router: $ ri-admin host drain --host host-123
  2. Collect kernel logs and GPU traces.
  3. If OOM, lower batch size and mark model config with a reduced max_batch_size.
  4. Reboot host only if necessary and follow post-reboot health checks.

- Runbook: degraded batch throughput
  1. Inspect scheduling-daemon metrics for batch-formation rate.
  2. Verify kernel-selector cache hit rate; if low, warm cache using bench-runner warmup.
  3. Temporarily increase max_latency_window_ms and monitor impact.

9) Team wiki and ownership
- Primary owners: serving-runtime (team alias: @serving-runtime).
- Secondary: eng-sre for capacity and incident response; eng-platform for rollout and dashboards.
- Useful links:
  - Runtime reference: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/serving-runtime-reference-2026-03-04
  - Ops playbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/serving-runtime-ops-playbook-2026-03-20
  - Kernel selector design doc: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/serving-runtime-architecture-kernel-scheduling-playbook-2026-03-15

10) Ownership, SLOs, and alerting thresholds
- SLOs (example):
  - small-models (<= 7B): p99 <= 120ms, error rate < 0.1%
  - medium-models (7B-30B): p99 <= 300ms, error rate < 0.2%
  - large-models (>30B): p99 <= 800ms, error rate < 0.5%
- Alerts (examples):
  - p99 latency > SLO for 15 minutes -> P1 alert to serving-runtime and eng-sre.
  - kernel-selector error rate increase > 0.5% over baseline -> P2.

Appendix A — Example configs
- kernel-selector config (excerpt):
  default_policy: "latency-first"
  policies:
    latency-first:
      prefer_variants: ["fp16_direct_attn", "int8_fast"]
      max_selection_time_ms: 5

Appendix B — Troubleshooting checklist
- If latency spikes: check kernel logs, profile, check cache miss rates, check mixed GPU generations.
- If throughput drops: warm kernel cache, re-evaluate batcher knobs, inspect scheduling queue metrics.

Document maintenance
- Owner must review this document quarterly or after any major release.
- Tag release entries with PR and ticket numbers when adding to the release notes section.
